title: Candidate assessment
goal: Read one candidate's result as expected versus actual, per skill, closed by the verdict.
primaryQuestion: Where does this candidate sit against the profile's expectations?
_why: The screen that proves the model's second invariant: expected and actual proficiency are two columns, and deviations in BOTH directions are shown with equal weight — a candidate above expectations on three skills and below on one reads exactly like that, not as 'fine overall'. The header carries the candidate's name ONLY (no text under titles, system rule); the profile and the target seniority are the first two rows of the verdict Descriptions — two axes, two rows.

zones.name: verdict
zones.answers: Where does this candidate sit against the profile's expectations?
zones.purpose: Two cards side by side. Left, Descriptions: first the profile and the target seniority (two axes, two rows), then the verdict — the seniority the candidate reads as, the decision, the notes — placeholder text naming each field. Right, two Stat counters: how many assessed skills fall below the expected proficiency (gaps) and how many rise above it (surpluses), plain numbers with equal visual weight.

zones.name: assessment
zones.purpose: One Table row per assessed skill: the skill's name, Expected (the profile's expected proficiency at the target seniority, a Badge), Actual (what the interview showed, a Badge), and the delta as an Icon arrow with both proficiency names spelled out — 'Advanced → Expert', never a bare number, never one merged string. Up and down get the same treatment.

states.empty: EmptyState surface=page icon=person when the candidate id in the URL matches nothing: says so and offers the way back to Candidates.
states.error: The same EmptyState as the empty state: a bad deep link is the only broken state a static reader has.

data: per skill: expected proficiency (from the profile), actual proficiency (from the assessment)
verdict: seniority, decision, notes; gap and surplus counts derived, never stored

behaviours.given: a candidate assessed above the expectation on some skills and below it on others
behaviours.then: both directions are counted and returned separately — gaps and surpluses — neither folded into the other nor into a single score
behaviours.why: The point of keeping expected and actual apart is to see both kinds of deviation; a single 'fit score' would re-merge what the model just separated.
